141.title: Benediction and the Tantum Ergo
141.hook: a blessing with the monstrance, and a hymn written by Aquinas
141.howItsDone: Benediction usually closes a time of Eucharistic adoration: the people sing the Tantum Ergo, the priest or deacon blesses them with the monstrance in silence while a bell rings, and the host is returned to the tabernacle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the holy hour, and the question in the garden. Your line was watch one hour.

At the end of adoration, something changes in the room. Incense rises. People who've been sitting quietly for an hour stand and start to sing, in Latin, a slow old melody. The priest puts on a long shawl that covers his hands. He lifts the gold monstrance and turns to face everyone. A bell rings. And instead of the people coming to the Eucharist, it's as if the Eucharist comes to them.
screen: `INCENSE RISES.` → `A SLOW LATIN SONG.` → `THE MONSTRANCE TURNS TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Benediction comes from Latin, bene, well, and dicere, to say: a blessing, a speaking well. It's the name for the short service that usually closes Eucharistic adoration. Here's its shape. The people sing a hymn, often the Tantum Ergo. The priest incenses the host. After a prayer, he wraps his hands in the humeral veil, that long shawl, so it's clear the blessing comes from the Eucharist, not from him. He lifts the monstrance and makes the sign of the cross with it over the people, in silence, while a bell rings. Then the host is returned to the tabernacle. The hymn is worth knowing. Tantum Ergo is the last two verses of a longer hymn, Pange Lingua, written by Thomas Aquinas, the great thirteenth-century theologian, for the new feast of Corpus Christi. Tradition says the Pope asked him to compose the prayers for that feast. It opens: "Tantum ergo Sacramentum veneremur cernui." Roughly: so great a sacrament, let us bow down and worship. Then it says, in effect, that faith fills in where the senses fail: what the eyes can't see, faith supplies. Aquinas wrote enormous books of careful reasoning, and his early biographers report that near the end of his life he stopped writing, saying all he'd written seemed like straw compared to what he had seen. Here, in a short hymn, the thinker bows. That's the spirit of Benediction: after the watching, you don't reach for the blessing. You stand still, and it comes to you.
screen: `BENE DICERE: TO SPEAK WELL.` · `THE VEIL, THE SIGN OF THE CROSS.` · `AQUINAS WROTE THE HYMN.` · `FAITH SUPPLIES WHAT EYES CAN'T SEE.` · then, large: `TANTUM ERGO SACRAMENTUM.`

segments.voice: Sit or stand still, hands open on your knees or at your sides, and picture the moment the monstrance is lifted toward you, or simply a warm light turning your way. You don't earn it, and you don't reach for it; you stay still and let it come. If you pray, you can bow your head.
Benediction. From the Latin for speaking well. The blessing with the monstrance that closes adoration, sung in with Aquinas's Tantum Ergo. Today's word.
Your line: the blessing comes to you. What the eyes can't see, faith supplies. Go gently.

142.title: Spiritual communion
142.hook: when you can't receive, you can ask to be united in desire
142.howItsDone: Catholics who can't receive Communion, whether sick, far from a church, or not able to receive at a given Mass, often make a spiritual communion, many using Alphonsus Liguori's short prayer or their own words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Benediction, and Aquinas's Tantum Ergo. Your line was the blessing comes to you.

Spring 2020. Churches around the world locked their doors. Millions of Catholics who had received Communion every Sunday of their lives were suddenly watching Mass on a laptop at the kitchen table. The priest held up the host on a grainy screen, and there was nothing to walk forward to. Many of them, at that moment, did something their grandparents knew well but they had barely heard of. They closed their eyes and asked to receive him anyway, without bread.
screen: `SPRING 2020, CHURCHES LOCKED.` → `MASS ON A LAPTOP.` → `NOTHING TO WALK FORWARD TO.`

segments.voice: Spiritual communion is the old Catholic practice of uniting yourself to Jesus in the Eucharist by desire, when you can't receive him in the sacrament. It isn't new, and it isn't only for emergencies. The Council of Trent, in the 1500s, spoke of people who receive spiritually, eating by desire, through a living faith. Thomas Aquinas taught that the effect of the sacrament can be received by desire, the way a person who longs for baptism is already turned toward it. Who uses it? The sick who can't get to church. People in places with no priest. Those who, for reasons of Church teaching, aren't able to receive Communion at a given time: they can still come to Mass and make a spiritual communion. Non-Catholics at a Catholic Mass sometimes do this too, in their own way. And many Catholics make one every day, at home, outside of Mass. Saints have loved it. Alphonsus Liguori, an eighteenth-century Italian bishop, wrote a short prayer for it that's still widely used. In essence: I believe you are present in the Blessed Sacrament; I love you above all things and desire to receive you; since I can't now receive you sacramentally, come at least spiritually into my heart; I embrace you as if you were already there, and never let me be separated from you. Catholics are clear it isn't the same as receiving the sacrament. It's a longing, not a substitute. But they also say longing is not nothing. A desire turned toward God is already a kind of opening. That's the week in adoration: the tabernacle, the monstrance, the holy hour, Benediction, and now this.
screen: `UNITED BY DESIRE.` · `TRENT AND AQUINAS TAUGHT IT.` · `THE SICK, THE FAR, THE WAITING.` · `A LONGING, NOT A SUBSTITUTE.` · then, large: `DESIRE IS A DOOR.`

segments.voice: If you're Catholic, use Alphonsus Liguori's prayer if you know it, or say the same thing simply in your own words: that you believe, that you long for him, and that you ask him to come into your heart; then stay quiet, as you would after receiving. If you're not Catholic, think of something or someone you long for but can't reach right now, and notice that the longing itself is a kind of closeness.
Spiritual communion. Uniting yourself to Jesus in the Eucharist by desire, when you can't receive him in the sacrament. Today's word.
Your line: desire is a door. Tomorrow, the liturgical year begins. That's day one hundred forty-two.

143.title: The colors of the year
143.hook: violet, white, green, red, and rose twice a year
143.howItsDone: Catholic priests change the color of their vestments with the seasons: violet in Advent and Lent, white at Christmas and Easter, green in Ordinary Time, red for Pentecost and martyrs, and, where a parish keeps the custom, rose on two Sundays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, spiritual communion, united by desire. Your line was desire is a door.

Go to Mass every Sunday for a year and watch just one thing, the color the priest wears, and a pattern appears. Green, week after week. Then a sudden purple. Then bright white and gold. Then purple again, longer this time. White for weeks. A flash of red. Then back to green for months. And on two Sundays, in parishes that keep the custom, pink. It isn't fashion. It's a calendar you can read from the back pew. Today's word: the liturgical year.
screen: `GREEN, WEEK AFTER WEEK.` → `THEN PURPLE, THEN WHITE.` → `A CALENDAR FROM THE BACK PEW.`

segments.voice: The liturgical year is the Church's own calendar. It doesn't start in January. It starts on the first Sunday of Advent, about four weeks before Christmas, and every year it walks through the whole life of Christ: waiting for him, his birth, his ministry, his death, his resurrection, the coming of the Spirit, and then the long life of the Church. Each season has a color, and the priest's vestments and the altar cloths change to match. Violet, a deep purple, is for waiting and turning: Advent and Lent. White, sometimes gold, is for joy and light: Christmas, Easter, feasts of Jesus and Mary, and saints who weren't martyrs. Green is for growth: Ordinary Time, the longest stretch of the year. Red is for fire and blood: Pentecost, when the Spirit came like fire, Palm Sunday, Good Friday and the feasts of martyrs. Then rose, a soft pink, which may be worn on just two Sundays: the third Sunday of Advent and the fourth Sunday of Lent. They're named after the first word of the old Latin entrance chant: Gaudete, rejoice, in Advent, and Laetare, be joyful, in Lent. A break in the middle of a hard season, a glimpse of the joy ahead. Gaudete comes from Paul's letter to the Philippians, which in the Douay-Rheims says: "Rejoice in the Lord always; again, I say, rejoice." So the colors aren't decoration. They teach time. For Catholics, the year isn't just one thing after another. It's a story you live inside, and it tells you where you are.
screen: `THE YEAR STARTS IN ADVENT.` · `VIOLET, WHITE, GREEN, RED.` · `ROSE: GAUDETE AND LAETARE.` · `COLORS THAT TEACH TIME.` · then, large: `REJOICE IN THE LORD ALWAYS.`

segments.voice: Picture the color of the Church's season right now filling the room; if you don't know it, guess, or choose green, the color of ordinary days. Then ask what color your own life is right now: waiting violet, joyful white, growing green, burning red? Don't judge it, just name it, and if you pray, offer that color to God as it is.
Liturgical year. The Church's own calendar, starting in Advent, walking through the life of Christ, with a color for each season. Today's word.

144.title: Advent
144.hook: four weeks of waiting, a wreath of four candles, one lit each Sunday
144.howItsDone: In Advent, Catholic churches turn violet, and some families keep an Advent wreath at home, lighting one more of its four candles each Sunday, often with a short Scripture reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the liturgical year and its colors. Your line was time has colors.

Early December. The stores have been playing Christmas music since before Halloween. Every screen says buy, hurry, celebrate now. Then you walk into a Catholic church and it's quiet, and purple, and there's no Christmas tree yet. Just a ring of evergreen with four candles, and only one of them lit. It can feel stubborn, like the Church missed the memo. It's on purpose. Before the feast, the Church asks for something the rest of December has almost forgotten how to do. Today: Advent.
screen: `CHRISTMAS MUSIC SINCE OCTOBER.` → `A QUIET, PURPLE CHURCH.` → `ONE CANDLE OF FOUR.`

segments.voice: Advent comes from the Latin adventus, a coming or an arrival. In the Roman world it was used for an emperor arriving to visit a city. Christians used it for the coming of Christ. Advent begins four Sundays before Christmas, the first season of the Church year, and it looks two ways at once. The first part looks ahead to the end of time, when Christians believe Christ will come again. The last part, especially from December seventeenth, looks back to his first coming, at Bethlehem. So Advent waits for someone who has come, and who is still coming. The Advent wreath is a later custom, and a lovely one. A popular story traces it to Johann Wichern, a Lutheran pastor in Hamburg in the 1830s, who put candles on a cartwheel so the children in his orphanage could count down the days. The idea spread, and Catholics took it up too. Today it's usually a circle of evergreen with four candles, three violet and one rose, one more lit each Sunday. The rose one is for the third Sunday, Gaudete, the rejoicing from yesterday. Advent is a season of preparing, penitential but not grim. The prophet Isaiah is read a lot, promising light to people in darkness. People sing the old hymn O come, O come, Emmanuel, built on antiphons the Church prays in the last days before Christmas. Families keep the wait in their own ways. Filipino Catholics have Simbang Gabi, nine Masses before dawn, starting December sixteenth. In Mexico and across Latin America there's Las Posadas: nine nights of neighbors acting out Mary and Joseph knocking at doors, asking for room. The whole season practices a skill December makes hard: waiting without rushing, and letting wanting grow.
screen: `ADVENTUS: AN ARRIVAL.` · `HE HAS COME, AND IS COMING.` · `A WREATH: THREE VIOLET, ONE ROSE.` · `WAITING WITHOUT RUSHING.` · then, large: `WAIT WELL.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle and can light it safely, do; if not, picture one, and watch the flame. Think of something you're waiting for right now, news, a person, healing, a change, and let the waiting be quiet, not anxious. If you pray, offer the waiting to God; if you don't, just keep the flame company.
Advent. From the Latin for an arrival. Four weeks of waiting before Christmas, one candle more each Sunday. Today's word.
Your line: wait well. A long line can be a small Advent. See you tomorrow.

145.title: Christmas is a season
145.hook: the octave and the season run on to the Baptism of the Lord
145.howItsDone: Catholics keep Christmas as a season: churches stay decorated and white vestments are worn through the octave and the twelve days until the Baptism of the Lord, and some families leave the tree and crib up until then.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Advent, waiting for someone who has come and is still coming. Your line was wait well.

December twenty-sixth. The wrapping paper's in the recycling. The radio has abruptly stopped playing carols. By New Year's, trees lie on the curb, needles everywhere. For most of the culture, Christmas is one day, and the day after, it's over. But walk into a Catholic church on December twenty-sixth, or on January fifth, and the tree is still lit, the crib is still there, the priest is still in white, and people are still singing Christmas hymns. The party hasn't ended. It's barely started.
screen: `DECEMBER 26: TREES ON THE CURB.` → `IN CHURCH, STILL WHITE.` → `THE PARTY HAS BARELY STARTED.`

segments.voice: In the Church's calendar, Christmas is a season, not a day. It begins on Christmas Eve and runs until the feast of the Baptism of the Lord, in early to mid January. Inside it are three layers. First, the octave. The Church gives Christmas and Easter an octave: the celebration lasts eight days, as if it's all one long day of joy. The Christmas octave runs from December twenty-fifth to January first, which Catholics keep as the Solemnity of Mary, the Mother of God. Second, the twelve days, the old count from Christmas to the Epiphany on January sixth, the one in the song. Third, the full season, running on to the Baptism of the Lord, when the adult Jesus stands in the Jordan; the next day, Ordinary Time begins. Following an old custom, some families keep their crib up even longer, until Candlemas on February second. The word itself is simple: Christmas is Christ's Mass, from old English, named after the Mass. Why so long? One answer is in Luke. After the shepherds came and went, the Douay-Rheims says: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." She didn't move on. She kept turning it over, and the Church asks the same. The feast is too big for one day, so the days after it are full of feasts: Stephen, whom tradition calls the first martyr, John the apostle, the Holy Innocents, the Holy Family. The whole season is a slow pondering of one astonishing claim: God was born.
screen: `A SEASON, NOT A DAY.` · `THE OCTAVE: EIGHT DAYS AS ONE.` · `TWELVE DAYS TO EPIPHANY.` · `ON TO THE BAPTISM OF THE LORD.` · then, large: `MARY KEPT ALL THESE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing from Christmas, this past one or the next, that you could keep going a little longer: a light in the window, a song, a habit of calling someone, a crib on a shelf. Picture it still there in the middle of January, still celebrating when everyone else has stopped. If you pray, ponder one line of the Christmas story, the way Mary did.
Octave. Eight days kept as one long day of joy, the Christmas octave running from December twenty-fifth to January first. Today's word.
Your line: Christmas isn't one day. An octave, twelve days, a whole season. That's day one hundred forty-five.

146.title: Epiphany and the chalked door
146.hook: many families chalk C+M+B and the year above the door, for the magi and a blessing
146.howItsDone: On or near Epiphany some Catholic families bless their homes, chalking the year and C+M+B over the front door with blessed chalk, sometimes with a priest's visit or a short prayer said together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christmas as a season, octave and all. Your line was Christmas isn't one day.

Walk down certain streets in January, in Poland, Germany, Austria, or a Catholic neighborhood in Chicago, and look above the front doors. Scrawled in chalk on the lintel: a string of letters and numbers, with little crosses between them. Something like twenty, C, M, B, twenty-six. It looks like graffiti, or a code. It's neither. The family wrote it there, on or near one particular feast, and it stays up all year, slowly fading.
screen: `CHALK ABOVE THE DOOR.` → `20 + C + M + B + 26.` → `A CODE THAT ISN'T A CODE.`

segments.voice: Epiphany comes from the Greek epiphaneia, an appearing, a showing forth. It's the feast of January sixth; in some countries, including the United States, it's kept on a Sunday in early January. It celebrates the magi, the wise men from the East who followed a star to find the child. Matthew tells it this way, in the Douay-Rheims: "And entering into the house, they found the child with Mary his mother, and falling down they adored him: and opening their treasures, they offered him gifts; gold, frankincense, and myrrh." For the Church, it's the moment Christ is shown to the whole world, not only to Israel, since the magi were foreigners. Notice: Matthew never says there were three, and never calls them kings. The number three probably comes from the three gifts, and the names Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar come from later tradition, not the Bible. In Eastern churches the same day, called Theophany, focuses mostly on Jesus's baptism instead. Now the chalk. On Epiphany some Catholic families bless their homes. Chalk is blessed, often at the parish, and someone writes over the front door the first two digits of the year, then C, M and B with crosses between, then the last two digits. C, M, B are the initials of the three traditional names, and also of a short Latin blessing: Christus mansionem benedicat. Christ bless this house. The little crosses are signs of the cross. Some children go door to door dressed as the three kings, singing, chalking houses and collecting money for the poor. The chalk wears away over the year, which is part of the point. Every January, you bless the door again.

147.title: Ordinary Time
147.hook: ordinary means counted Sundays, the long green growing season
147.howItsDone: In Ordinary Time Catholic priests wear green, the Sundays are numbered, and the Gospel readings walk through Jesus's public ministry week by week.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Epiphany, and C, M, B chalked above the door. Your line was Christ bless this house.

Most of life isn't a feast. It's Tuesday. Laundry, emails, the commute, a sandwich at your desk, the same argument about the dishes. The holy parts of life seem to be the big days: weddings, funerals, Christmas morning. Everything else is filler. The Catholic calendar has a name for most of the year, and people laugh a little when they first hear it, because it sounds so plain. It's the longest season of all, and it comes around twice. Today: Ordinary Time.
screen: `MOST OF LIFE IS TUESDAY.` → `THE BIG DAYS, AND THE FILLER.` → `THE LONGEST SEASON.`

segments.voice: Here's the surprise: ordinary doesn't mean plain or boring. It comes from ordinal, as in counted: first, second, third. The weeks of this season are numbered: the Third Sunday in Ordinary Time, the Twenty-Fifth Sunday, and so on. In Latin the season is called tempus per annum, time through the year. There are thirty-three or thirty-four of these weeks, in two stretches. The first is short, from the Baptism of the Lord until Ash Wednesday. The second is long, from after Pentecost all the way to Advent, most of the summer and fall, ending with the feast of Christ the King. The color is green, the color of things growing. Week by week, the Sunday Gospels walk steadily through Jesus's public life: his parables, his healings, his teaching. After the great feasts show who Jesus is, Ordinary Time is about following him on regular days. Paul put it this way, in the Douay-Rheims: "All whatsoever you do in word or in work, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God and the Father by him." Catholics have loved saints who made ordinary work holy. Brother Lawrence, a seventeenth-century Carmelite, spent years as the cook in a Paris monastery, and said he felt as close to God among the pots and pans as when kneeling in church. Thérèse of Lisieux called her way the little way: small things done with great love. That's the spirit of the green season. Not waiting for a feast. Growing, week by week.
screen: `ORDINARY MEANS COUNTED.` · `TWO STRETCHES, GREEN.` · `FOLLOWING ON REGULAR DAYS.` · `GOD AMONG THE POTS AND PANS.` · then, large: `GREEN, GROWING.`

segments.voice: Think of one job you'll do today that you usually rush through: washing dishes, answering email, folding clothes, driving. Picture doing it slowly, with attention, even with care. If you pray, offer it to God before you start, the way Brother Lawrence did with his pots and pans; if you don't, just decide to do it well, for someone.
Ordinary Time. Not plain time, but counted time: the long green season of numbered Sundays, twice a year. Today's word.
Your line: green, growing. Your week: Benediction, spiritual communion, the colors, Advent, Christmas as a season, Epiphany, and Ordinary Time. A full week, done.
